findings.title: The once-in-12-months limit does not reach a rent rise made by a further agreement
findings.provision: ss. 30(1), 31B(1)-(3) (s. 31B as replaced by the Residential Tenancies Amendment Act 2024 s. 27)
findings.external_source: The brief for this run (4 October 2026). The human asked whether Western Australia's once-in-12-months limit on rent increases can be avoided by ending a tenancy and starting another, as Queensland's 2023 limit could be (ABC News, 12 October 2023) until Queensland attached it to the premises in 2024; the encoder's brief then named the consecutive agreements to examine: the same parties, different tenants, a gap between agreements, fixed term to periodic, periodic to fixed term, and a rent set by a new agreement against an increase by notice under s 30. This candidate's question, named there: whether a rent set by a new agreement between the same parties is limited as an increase by notice under s 30 is, and so whether the limit can be avoided by renewing.
findings.summary: Section 30(1) limits increases of rent by notice: 60 clear days' notice, and no increase within 12 months of the tenancy's start or the last increase. Section 31B, which the 2024 Act put in place of the former s 31B, treats a further agreement between the same parties as a continuation only 'for the purposes of working out' when rent was last increased under s 30 or the method last changed under s 31A. A rent that the further agreement itself fixes is not an increase under s 30 (FK-01, reading taken), so on the text a lessor and tenant may agree a higher rent at every renewal, at any interval and without notice: six-monthly fixed terms at $500, $550 and $600 are lawful (cases section F) where the same rises by notice under one agreement are not. The bond can follow at each renewal, since a new agreement takes its own bond under s 29 at its own rent, while s 31 lets the bond rise only on a notice of increase. The explanatory memorandum for Bill 140 gave the purpose of the new s 31B as keeping the 12-month minimum where the parties make consecutive agreements, and both second reading speeches told Parliament that a tenant renewing in the same property would be treated as under one continuing agreement, so that the rent could not rise within 12 months of the last increase. The former s 31B (inserted in 2011) at least deferred, for 30 days, a rise made by a renegotiated lease; the 2024 replacement dropped that rule and put nothing in its place for a rise made by the new agreement. Queensland's 2023 text stated the same gap in a note to its s 91; its 2024 text closed it by attaching the 12 months to the premises. Whether this is the Act's meaning turns on FK-01 (candidate U-02).

findings.title: Whether a rent fixed by a continuing agreement is an 'increase' is left open
findings.external_source: The brief for this run (4 October 2026): before the encoding began, the orchestrating session's own reading of ss 30 and 31B raised whether a rent fixed by a renewal is an 'increase' at all.
findings.summary: The encoding takes FK-01 reading A: a rent that a further agreement fixes is not an increase under s 30, and s 31B carries across only increases by notice (M-01). Reading B is arguable: s 31B(2) says the continuing agreement 'is taken to be a continuation' of the existing one, so a higher rent under it is an increase of the rent payable under the continued agreement made otherwise than under s 30, which 'shall not' happen (s 30(1)), and s 82(1)(a) avoids the excess. The Act's own vocabulary of renewal points both ways. Sections 5(1), 93(1)(a) and 99(2) ('entered into, or last renewed or extended'; 'the original, renewed or extended term') and r 5AC ('the agreement is renewed or extended') treat a renewal as something done to an agreement, the same agreement with a new term, so that a higher rent on renewal would be a variation of the rent payable under it; s 31B treats a renewal as a new agreement deemed a continuation for limited purposes. 'Renewal' is not defined. The choice decides whether every renewal may carry an unlimited rise (A) or none may within 12 months of the last increase (B). The Interpretation Act s 18 (a construction promoting the purpose is preferred) and the extrinsic material favour B; the words of s 31B(1) favour A. The assertions show the two readings parting on the same facts (A2, F2).

findings.summary: Because s 31B carries across only the day of the last increase by notice, and the 12 months in s 30(1)(b) run from that day, a continuing agreement can raise the rent at its start, by its own terms, and again by notice soon after. Had A2 not been a continuation (a one-day gap, or FK-16 reading B), the 12 months would run from A2's own start and the second rise could not take effect before 1 January 2028. The provision meant to protect tenants across consecutive agreements makes the second rise come sooner. Under one agreement the same two rises two months apart are not possible: a second increase under A1 two months after the first fails s 30(1)(b).

findings.title: No provision ends an agreement that the parties replace while the tenant stays
findings.external_source: The brief for this run (4 October 2026). The human asked whether Western Australia's once-in-12-months limit on rent increases can be avoided by ending a tenancy and starting another, as Queensland's 2023 limit could be (ABC News, 12 October 2023) until Queensland attached it to the premises in 2024; the encoder's brief then named the consecutive agreements to examine: the same parties, different tenants, a gap between agreements, fixed term to periodic, periodic to fixed term, and a rent set by a new agreement against an increase by notice under s 30. This candidate's question, named there: what becomes of the existing agreement in consecutive agreements between the same parties, fixed term to periodic and periodic to fixed term, when the tenant stays.
findings.summary: Section 60(1) says an agreement 'shall not terminate or be terminated except' in the circumstances it lists, 'Despite any Act or law to the contrary'. None fits the commonest way a tenancy is renewed: the parties make a new agreement and the tenant stays. Paragraph (g) needs vacant possession delivered up, and the opening words shut out surrender by operation of law. So the old agreement stays in force beside the new one: a fixed term continues under s 76C as a periodic tenancy (cases section A), and a periodic tenancy simply continues (section E(i)). Two agreements between the same parties for the same premises are then in force at once, at different rents (W1 at $500 and W2 at $600 on 1 September 2026). Consequences the text does not resolve: the surviving periodic agreement can be ended without a ground under s 64 during the new agreement's fixed term, when s 64(5) bars that notice under the new one; s 31B(2)(c) can never be met for a periodic agreement replaced in place, because its term never ends, so a periodic-to-fixed renewal in place is never a continuation; a notice of increase could be given under either agreement; references to 'the residential tenancy agreement' to which the lessor or tenant is a party (s 3A(2), s 26A) have two candidates; and s 29(1)(a), which forbids more than one bond 'in relation to any residential tenancy agreement', allows one under each. A court might avoid all this by treating the new agreement as a variation of the old, but a variation that raises the rent is then an increase made otherwise than under s 30 (U-02).

findings.title: A new tenant starts a fresh 12 months, so the limit can be avoided by ending the tenancy and re-letting
findings.external_source: The brief for this run (4 October 2026). The human asked whether Western Australia's once-in-12-months limit on rent increases can be avoided by ending a tenancy and starting another, as Queensland's 2023 limit could be (ABC News, 12 October 2023) until Queensland attached it to the premises in 2024; the encoder's brief then named the consecutive agreements to examine: the same parties, different tenants, a gap between agreements, fixed term to periodic, periodic to fixed term, and a rent set by a new agreement against an increase by notice under s 30. findings.summary: The 12 months in s 30(1)(b) run from the commencement of 'the tenancy' or the last increase under it, and s 31B carries them across only to an agreement 'between the same parties' (s 31B(3): the same lessor and at least one tenant in common). A lessor of a periodic tenancy may give notice without a ground (s 64: 60 clear days) and, once the tenant has gone, let the premises the next day to someone else at any rent, with a fresh 12 months. In the evidence, a tenancy whose rent rose to $550 on 1 January 2026 is ended without a ground on 1 May 2026 and the premises let on 2 May at $700; on either reading of FK-01 nothing limits the $700, though under the first tenancy the rent could not have risen again before 1 January 2027. The same follows where a buyer of the premises lets them to a new tenant. Section 26A reaches the ending only where a matter in s 26B(2) motivated it. This is the route the human's brief asked about: Queensland's 2023 limit, which ran 'for the agreement', could be avoided this way, and Queensland's 2024 text runs it 'for the residential premises' across agreements, tenants and owners. The 2024 Western Australian amendment was described to Parliament only in terms of tenants who renew in the same property; whether a limit on the premises was considered is not in the extrinsic material held.

findings.summary: For s 31B(2)(a) the agreements are between the same parties if 'the tenant, or at least 1 co-tenant, is the same under both agreements'. The two limbs follow s 3 'party' (a)(ii) (one tenant: 'the tenant under the agreement') and (a)(iii) (two or more: 'each co-tenant'). Where one agreement has a single tenant and the other has co-tenants (a tenant renews with a partner added, or one of two flatmates renews alone), read word for word neither 'the tenant' nor 'at least 1 co-tenant' is the same under both, and the new agreement is not a continuation. The encoding counts any tenant in common, which is the likely purpose, without recording a fork. The evidence shows both: Y2 (T1 and T2) continues Y1 (T1 alone), and Y4 (T2 alone) continues Y3 (T1 and T2), on the encoding, and neither does on the literal words, which agree with the encoding where the line-up stays single or stays plural. The difference decides when the next increase may take effect and, on FK-01 reading B, whether a renewal rent is limited at all. Such changes at renewal are common.

findings.summary: Section 70A(2) says the term of an agreement 'does not end on the expiry day unless' a notice under s 70A was given. In the commonest renewal no such notice is given: the parties sign a new fixed term to start the day after the old one's expiry day. On FK-16 reading B the old term has not ended (s 76C continues the agreement as a periodic tenancy), so the new agreement does not start 'immediately after the end of the term' and is never a continuation; on reading A, taken, the term ends on the expiry day whether or not s 76C continues the agreement. The note to s 31B(2) points to s 76C without saying which. The former s 31B (2011) spoke of the end of the term 'whether under the terms of the agreement or under section 76C'; the 2024 text dropped those words. In section A the renewal continues the old agreement on A and not on B, and an increase by notice under it from 3 March 2027 is good on A and fails on B.

findings.title: An order under s 32 may run from a day before it is made, with nothing to recover the excess already paid
findings.summary: The court may order that 'from a specified day, which may be a day earlier than the date of the application by the tenant', the rent shall not exceed a specified amount (s 32(4)). The order has effect for a period 'commencing on the day on which the order is made' (s 32(5)), and demanding or receiving rent above it is an offence (s 32(7)). For the time between the specified day and the order, rent above the amount has already been received, lawfully when received; the section neither makes the excess repayable nor says how s 32(7) applies to it. The console scheme, like the encoding, runs an order from the day it is made (its design note (5)); writing the scheme raised the question.

findings.title: The prescribed form and the 2011 explanatory memorandum ask for a day more notice than s 70A(3)
findings.summary: Section 70A(3): the notice 'must be given not later than 30 days before the possession day', that is, on or before the 30th day before (the Interpretation Act s 61(1)(c)). findings.title: 'Method' and 'means'; and a notice under s 31A called a 'notice of increase' even when it lowers the rent
findings.summary: Section 31A(1) and (2) speak of 'the method' of calculating income-based rent; s 31A(2)(b)(ii) and s 31B(1)(b) of 'the means of calculating rent'. Sections 31(1A) ('notice of increase in rent'), 100(4) and r 5CB(1AA)(a) ('notice of increase of rent') give that name to every notice under s 31A, including one whose change of method lowers the rent, while s 32(2)(a)(ii) speaks of 'a change in the method of calculating rent that results in an increase'.
